extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in leadership (scholars, practitioners, students, and the informed public)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or judging public apologies/expressions of regret by leaders—when they are appropriate, what makes them meaningful, and what features (acknowledgement, learning, candor) matter. Focuses especially on high-ranking public/military officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apology versus expression of regret
rubrics_metrics.description: Milley’s statement was 'not precisely an apology, rather it was an expression of deep regret.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between a full apology and expressions of regret or contrition; an expression of regret may acknowledge feeling sorry without performing the full corrective or responsibility-taking acts of an apology. Evaluate statements for whether they rise to an apology or remain in the register of regret.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to acknowledge that one was wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: It was a supremely important gesture – the willingness of a man so highly placed publicly to acknowledge that what he did was wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A core component of an effective apology is an explicit admission that the action was wrong. The public acknowledgement itself is a key signal of responsibility and moral recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public nature and rank amplify significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The willingness of a man so highly placed publicly to acknowledge that what he did was wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When high-ranking officials (e.g., the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs) acknowledge mistakes publicly, the gesture carries extra weight and symbolic importance; assess apologies more heavily when they come from persons in positions of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of learning or corrective intent
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘As a commissioned uniformed officer, it was a mistake that I have learned from.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective apologies or regret statements often include an indication that the speaker has learned from the mistake or intends to change behavior. Look for language that conveys remorse plus learning or corrective commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual appropriateness of apologizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to prior work 'When Should a Leader Apologize – and When Not.' The specific incident: walking alongside the president during a controversial visit to a damaged church near the White House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a leader should apologize depends on context; evaluate the circumstances (the action, public reaction, institutional roles) to judge if an apology is warranted or if another response is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor and speaking plainly about leadership/authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The parade in recent weeks of top military brass saying out loud what they really think and feel about the president ... is heartening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frank, candid speech by leaders—especially when it expresses honest judgment about superiors or contested events—is presented positively. Assess leaders for willingness to be forthright even when politically delicate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalization: training and development of leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: The American military does the best job, by far the best job, of any American institution or organization educating leaders, training leaders, and developing leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leadership quality is tied to institutional training and professional development. When judging leaders' responses (including apologies), consider the role of institutional norms and training in shaping appropriate conduct and accountability.
